The Best Scooter Day Rides in the UK for 2026

People still raise an eyebrow when I tell them I do most of my favourite rides on a maxi-scooter, but the best scooter day rides in the UK prove the doubters wrong every single time. A modern machine like the Honda Forza 750 will hold 70mph on a dual carriageway without breaking sweat, then trickle through a market town with its automatic gearbox doing all the thinking. For a relaxed single-day loop with a proper cafe stop and somewhere sensible to park, nothing beats it. Over the past few seasons I have refined a shortlist of achievable day rides within easy reach of our major cities, each one chosen for gentle scenic roads, good coffee and a car park that will not swallow your centre stand.

The beauty of a scooter day ride is that you never have to commit to a fortnight away. You can leave after breakfast, cover a hundred relaxed miles of proper countryside and be home for tea. That underseat storage swallows a flask, a spare layer and your lunch, and the step-through frame means you step off at the cafe without doing a yoga pose over a tall tank. If you are new to the format, my companion piece on how to tour on a maxi-scooter covers luggage and comfort in more detail.

Surrey Hills Loop from London (A25 and B2126)

If you live in or near the capital, the Surrey Hills is the obvious first choice for a scooter day ride. A relaxed 60-mile loop out through Dorking, along the A25 towards Guildford and back over the wooded lanes of the B2126 and B2127 near Wotton gives you rolling greensand ridges, dappled beech woods and almost no intimidating fast sections. The gradients are gentle, the corners are open and sighted, and the whole thing suits an automatic scooter beautifully because you simply roll on and off the throttle.

Box Hill is the honeypot. The Ryka's Cafe at the foot of the Zig Zag Road has been a biker institution for decades and there is masses of parking, though it gets busy on a sunny Sunday so aim for a mid-morning arrival. From the National Trust viewpoint at the top you look clear across the Weald, and it is a five-minute walk from where you leave the scooter. The weekend routes from London guide has more escapes in this direction if you want to extend the day.

South Downs and the A272 Cruise

The A272 is one of the great unsung roads of southern England, and it is tailor-made for a scooter. Running roughly west to east across Sussex, it flows through Petersfield, Midhurst and Haywards Heath with long sweeping bends, big skies and the chalk ridge of the South Downs as a backdrop. There is nothing frantic about it. You settle into a rhythm around 50mph and let the scenery do the work. A full there-and-back exploration is around 90 miles from the Hampshire end and never feels like hard graft.

Stop at Cocking or Cowdray near Midhurst for coffee, or drop south onto the smaller lanes towards the coast. My full South Downs motorcycle route breaks the whole area down. This is gentle, confidence-building riding on well-surfaced roads with plenty of pull-ins, exactly what a maxi-scooter was built for.

The secret to a great scooter day ride is to stop treating it as A to B and start treating it as a moving picnic. Plan the ride around the cafe, not the cafe around the ride, and you will enjoy every mile.

The Cotswolds on Two Wheels (A429 Fosse Way)

The Cotswolds is postcard England and the honey-stone villages were made for a leisurely scooter pootle. The A429, the old Roman Fosse Way, runs dead straight and then gently undulating through Stow-on-the-Wold and Moreton-in-Marsh, and it links up with a web of quiet B-roads around Bourton-on-the-Water and the Slaughters. A loop taking in Burford, Bibury and Stow comes in around 70 miles of easy, scenic riding with sensible speed limits that never punish a smaller machine.

Parking is the only thing to plan for, because the pretty villages fill up fast. Stow-on-the-Wold has a large pay-and-display just off the square, and Bourton-on-the-Water has good motorcycle-friendly parking on the edge of the village. Grab a coffee and a slab of cake at one of the many tearooms. My detailed Cotswolds touring routes guide has the full loop mapped out.

New Forest Gentle Wander

For sheer relaxation, the New Forest takes some beating on a scooter. The roads here are quiet, the limits are low, and you share the tarmac with wild ponies so a calm pace is compulsory rather than optional. A loop from Lyndhurst down to Beaulieu, across to Brockenhurst and out towards the coast at Lymington is around 40 to 50 miles of pure gentle wandering. There is no pressure, no fast dual carriageway, just heathland, ancient woodland and open forest lawns.

Beaulieu has the National Motor Museum if you fancy combining the ride with a proper day out, and there are cafes in Brockenhurst and Lyndhurst with easy scooter parking. The New Forest destination guide covers where to eat and park in more depth. This one is my go-to when I want a short, soul-soothing ride rather than a big day.

Peak District Fringes (A6 and Chatsworth)

You do not have to tackle the dramatic mountain passes to enjoy the Peak District on a scooter. The fringes offer plenty of scenery with far less of the tight, steep drama that can unsettle a heavier automatic. A loop from Bakewell along the A6 towards Matlock, then up to Chatsworth and back through the gentler eastern moors gives you honeyed stone villages, the grand Chatsworth estate and rolling limestone dales at a manageable pace of around 55 miles.

Bakewell is the natural hub with big car parks and, of course, the famous Bakewell pudding to reward your arrival. If you feel more adventurous another day, my Peak District roads guide covers the bigger passes, but for a relaxed scooter day the fringe roads are ideal.

Practical Scooter Day-Ride Tips

A few things make these rides run smoothly, and they apply whether you ride a Forza, a maxi from another brand or a smaller machine:

  • Fuel the night before. Start with a full tank so your first stop is a cafe, not a garage.
  • Pack a layer. British weather turns, and underseat storage means you have no excuse not to carry waterproofs.
  • Use a phone mount for navigation. A secure holder such as the Oxford CLIQR Phone Mount keeps your route in view and your hands on the bars.
  • Arrive early at honeypots. Box Hill, Bourton and Bakewell fill up. A mid-morning arrival means easy parking.
  • Keep the pace relaxed. The whole point of a scooter day ride is the flow. There is no prize for rushing.

Which Scooter for These Rides?

Any capable maxi-scooter will handle these loops with ease. The Honda Forza 750 is my personal pick for its motorway ability and long-legged comfort, but a smaller-capacity machine copes perfectly well on the gentler routes like the New Forest and Cotswolds. If you are stepping up towards something that blurs the line between scooter and motorcycle, the automatic ease still lets you focus entirely on the scenery. For riders who want a bit more of a motorcycle feel while keeping things manageable, a machine like the Honda NC750X with its DCT automatic option gives you the same relaxed shifting with more traditional styling.

Whichever you choose, the best scooter day rides in the UK all share the same recipe: gentle roads, glorious scenery, a proper cafe and no stress. Fill the flask, point the front wheel at the countryside and enjoy the ride.
keyTakeaways: Maxi-scooters handle relaxed day loops brilliantly: 70mph on dual carriageways, automatic ease through towns and underseat storage.
The Surrey Hills loop from London (60 miles) via the A25 and B2126 has gentle gradients and the Ryka's Cafe at Box Hill.
The A272 South Downs cruise is around 90 miles of sweeping bends at a relaxed 50mph.
The Cotswolds A429 Fosse Way loop (70 miles) and New Forest wander (40 to 50 miles) suit smaller machines too.
Fuel the night before, pack a layer, arrive early at honeypots and keep the pace relaxed.
